caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000017
attempts.entry_title: Choice, action and engagement across the mouse brain (Steinmetz et al. 2019)
attempts.summary: In this data the paper's engagement findings held up: pre-stimulus activity differs between task and passive states across the brain, and an engagement signal predicts whether the mouse responds. Visual coding was confined to visual areas and action coding was widespread, though one region had no action neurons. Choice coding restricted to frontal, basal ganglia and midbrain regions did not reproduce, possibly because the agent's kernel model admitted 2,886 neurons where the paper had about 4,240. The timing of choice signals was not tested, as the agent did not write that decoding. That Miss-trial visual responses stay within a visual pathway did not reproduce either, and several supplementary results missed.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Steinmetz, Zatka-Haas, Carandini and Harris (2019) on dandiset 000017, which holds Neuropixels recordings from 39 sessions of 10 mice performing a visual discrimination task, with passive replay. It covers the behaviour, the counts of neurons and regions, task responsiveness, the spread of activity after the stimulus, the pre-stimulus engagement signal, detect probability, the jPECC lead-lag analysis and the kernel regression. The decoding from kernel-model residuals was not run.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Steinmetz et al. (2019) from dandiset 000017

outcomes.statement: On high-contrast single-stimulus trials mice made 1.7 ± 2.5% incorrect choices and 10.1 ± 8.3% Misses (mean ± s.d. over 39 sessions of 10 mice).
outcomes.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1; Fig. 1c,d
outcomes.quote: Their choices were most accurate for high-contrast single stimuli (i.e. when the other stimulus was absent; 1.7 ± 2.5% incorrect choices, i.e. turns in the wrong direction; 10.1 ± 8.3% Misses, i.e. failures to turn; mean ± s.d., n = 39 sessions, 10 mice)
outcomes.notes: On engaged trials (reading b, the dataset's `included` flag) the means over 39 sessions are 1.71% incorrect choices (s.d. 2.47) and 10.12% Misses (s.d. 8.32), against 1.7 ± 2.5 and 10.1 ± 8.3. With all trials (reading a) Misses are 23.24%, outside tolerance; incorrect choices are 1.47%. Measured values are those of reading b, the reading that matches.
deviations: High contrast is 1.0, the highest of the dataset's four contrasts (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1); the dataset does not name the levels.

outcomes.statement: With low-contrast single stimuli mice made 5.1 ± 6.4% incorrect choices and 29.8 ± 19.8% Misses.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: with low-contrast single stimuli (5.1 ± 6.4% incorrect choices; 29.8 ± 19.8% Misses)
outcomes.notes: All trials (reading a) give 5.06% incorrect and 30.51% Misses (s.d. 6.42 and 19.87); engaged trials (b) give 5.07% and 29.84%. Both readings are within tolerance of 5.1 ± 6.4 and 29.8 ± 19.8.
deviations: Low contrast is 0.25, the lowest non-zero contrast of the dataset.

outcomes.statement: With competing stimuli of similar but unequal contrast (high against medium, medium against low) mice made 20.0 ± 7.9% incorrect choices and 13.9 ± 11.7% Misses.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: or with competing stimuli of similar but unequal contrast (20.0 ± 7.9% incorrect choices; 13.9 ± 11.7% Misses, on trials with high vs. medium or medium vs. low contrast)
outcomes.notes: All trials give 19.93% incorrect and 14.66% Misses; engaged trials 20.01% (s.d. 7.90) and 13.89% (s.d. 11.66). Expected 20.0 ± 7.9 and 13.9 ± 11.7; both readings match.
deviations: High against medium is 1.0 against 0.5, medium against low 0.5 against 0.25.

outcomes.statement: Reaction times were longer in the harder conditions (low-contrast single stimuli and competing stimuli of similar contrast) than for high-contrast single stimuli.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1; Fig. 1d
outcomes.quote: As expected, in these more challenging cases reaction times were longer ... multi-way ANOVA
outcomes.notes: On the Left and Right trials of definition T (trial reading b) the mean reaction times are 0.206 s (high-contrast single), 0.226 s (low-contrast single) and 0.221 s (competing); the condition factor has p = 2.9e-10 (F1, with session), 8.7e-09 (F2, with subject), and the contrast factor p = 9.6e-10 under F3 (competing-stimulus factor p = 0.017). The high-contrast class is fastest in every subject (medians). Under trial reading a (first detected movement after the stimulus, all trials with a Left or Right response) the condition p is 0.006 to 0.02 and the competing class is slightly faster than the high-contrast class (0.410 against 0.413 s), so the claim holds under reading b only.
deviations: The multi-way ANOVA is a type II ANOVA on an ordinary least squares fit (statsmodels); the paper names neither the software nor the sums of squares.

outcomes.statement: Choice decoded from instantaneous wheel velocity is at chance (47.7%) 50 ms before detected movement onset and near perfect (94.6%) 50 ms after it.
outcomes.source: Methods, Training protocol, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 1q
outcomes.quote: The decoder performed essentially at chance 50 ms prior to movement onset (47.7%) compared to near perfect performance 50 ms after movement onset (94.6%)
outcomes.notes: With the sign of the velocity (reading a), the mean accuracy over 39 sessions is 48.9% (s.d. 1.9) 50 ms before movement onset and 94.8% (s.d. 3.5) 50 ms after, against 47.7 and 94.6. 92.0% of trials have zero velocity at -50 ms. The logistic decoder (reading b) gives 59.0% before onset, outside tolerance, as it predicts the more frequent choice when velocity is zero; after onset it gives 94.7%. Reading a guesses (50%) where the velocity is zero, so its chance is 50% by construction; the chance of reading b, the more frequent choice per session, is 59.3% on average (50.0% to 74.5%), so both decoders are at chance before onset.
deviations: Velocities are taken at the nearest wheel sample (2.5 kHz) to each time; the logistic regression uses scikit-learn defaults, a standard choice.

outcomes.statement: On trials that ended in a Left or Right choice, mice turned the wheel within 400 ms of stimulus onset on 64.9 ± 14.0% (s.d.) of trials, nearly always (96.6 ± 3.4%) in the direction of their final choice.
outcomes.source: Methods, Training protocol, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: turning the wheel within 400 ms of stimulus appearance (64.9 ± 14.0% s.d., n=39 sessions), nearly always in the same direction as their final choice (96.6 ± 3.4%)
outcomes.notes: Reading a (first choice-amplitude turn, types 1 and 2) gives 61.48% (s.d. 12.00) of Left and Right response trials with a turn within 0.4 s, 95.78% (s.d. 3.86) of them in the response's direction; reading b (first movement of any kind) gives 67.49% and 94.93%. Both are within tolerance of 64.9 ± 14.0 and 96.6 ± 3.4.
deviations: All trials of each session are used, as the criterion says; the Methods passage does not say whether disengaged trials are dropped.

outcomes.statement: In the passive replay mice hardly ever turned the wheel; 94.1% ± 0.6% of passive trials with high-contrast stimuli had no movement.
outcomes.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: In these passive trials the mice hardly ever turned the wheel (94.1% ± 0.6% of trials with high contrast stimuli had no movement)
outcomes.notes: Of 3,410 passive presentations with contrast 1.0 on either side, 84.63% (mean over 39 sessions, s.e. 1.08) have no detected movement overlapping -0.05 to 0.4 s, and 84.96% for 0 to 0.4 s; pooled, 84.55% and 84.87%. Every reading is about 9 points below 94.1 ± 0.6. Subjects range from 78.3% to 91.5%. Movements are the dataset's detected wheel movements of any type, including small unclassified ones; the paper does not say what it counted as a movement here.
deviations: Movements are the dataset's `wheel_moves` intervals; findWheelMoves3 was not rerun on the wheel position.

outcomes.statement: Across 39 sessions in 10 mice with 92 probe insertions, 29,134 neurons were recorded (747 ± 38 per session, mean ± s.e.), 22,458 of them localized to one of 42 brain regions; the behaviour comprised 9,538 trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraphs 2 and 3; Fig. 1c legend
outcomes.quote: Across all sessions we recorded from 29,134 neurons (n=747 ± 38 neurons per session, mean ± s.e.), of which 22,458 were localizable to one of 42 brain regions
outcomes.notes: Units curated as single units with a trial firing rate of at least 0.1 Hz (reading b) number 29,283 (750.8 ± 38.0 per session, mean ± s.e.); 22,434 of them lie in the 42 regions (reading i) and 22,273 are neurons N (reading ii); 39 sessions, 10 mice, 92 probes. Engaged trials number 9,538, the paper's count; all trials 10,050. Reading a of neurons (all 33,997 curated units) is outside tolerance. With region labels as given (no parent mapping), 20,544 neurons lie in the 42 regions, also within tolerance.
deviations: Regions come from the location of each unit's peak channel (row peak_channel - 1 of the electrodes table), with finer Allen labels (SCig, SCsg, LSr, LSc, ORBm, COA, TT, PIR, DP) mapped to their parent among the 42 regions (an assumption, see supptable2-sessions).

outcomes.statement: Extended Data Table 1 gives, for each of the 42 regions, the number of recordings, mice, task-responsive neurons and neurons (for example MOs 19 recordings, 9 mice, 993 of 1,534 neurons responsive; MRN 11, 7, 722 of 857).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Table 1
outcomes.inferred: Numbers only in Extended Data Table 1; no sentence states them. The table's neuron column sums to 22,458 and its responsive column to 13,467, against 13,466 in the Results.
outcomes.notes: Re-run after the reader's answer (questions/steinmetz-2019.yaml), which found that the claims file misread the table and amended the criterion to count every neuron of the 42 regions (curated, at least 0.1 Hz), with recordings read as (a) sessions with any neuron of the region or (b) sessions with at least 13, and definition N as a variant. The first run tested definition N and found 26 of 42 regions matching, not reproduced. Under reading a, recordings, mice and neurons all match in 38 of 42 regions (recordings exact in 41, mice in 42, neurons within 10% in 38), the number needed for reproduced; the regions that differ are ACA, MOs, VPL and ZI (MOs has 18 recordings against 19 and 1,352 neurons against 1,534). The neurons number 22,434 and the active ones 13,532, against 22,458 and 13,467; active counts are within 10% in 36 regions. Reading b matches in 26 regions (recordings exact in 28), as does definition N. The measured value is the number of matching regions under reading a. With region labels as given (no parent mapping) 33 of 42 regions match (ACA, LS, MOs, OLF, ORB, SCm, SCs, VPL and ZI differ), partially reproduced under the criterion, so the outcome rests on the mapping of finer labels to their parent.
deviations: Assumption. Finer region labels (SCig, SCsg, LSr, LSc, ORBm, COA, TT, PIR, DP) are mapped to their parent among the 42 regions (Allen CCF hierarchy), as for recording-counts and supptable2-sessions; the paper does not say how labels were grouped, and the labels as given are run as a variant.
Mice are counted over every neuron of the region under both readings of the recordings; counted over the sessions of reading b they match in 38 regions.

outcomes.statement: The 39 sessions are those of Supplementary Table 2, each with its subject, date, age and recorded areas (for example Cori 2016-12-14, 11 weeks, ACA, CA3, DG, LS, MOs, SUB, VISp), from the 10 subjects of Supplementary Table 1 with their sex and genotype.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Tables 1 and 2
outcomes.inferred: Numbers only in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: All 39 sessions of the table are in the dataset, matched by subject and date, with matching ages (39 of 39) and sexes (10 of 10). Genotypes are the same lines named differently (Ai95 x VGlut1-Cre for RCL-GCaMP6f x VGlut-Cre, Vglut1-Cre for Vglut1-IRES2-Cre-D). The regions of each session's neurons (curated, at least 0.1 Hz) match the table's areas in 38 of 39 sessions under reading a, a region with any neuron in the session (Muller 2017-01-08 lacks MOs), and in 24 under reading b, a region with at least 13 neurons; neurons N give 24 as well. With region labels as given (no parent mapping) 25 of 39 match, so the outcome rests on the mapping. The reader's answer on edtable1-region-counts amended this criterion to take the area lists from the same neurons and readings as that claim; the first run had already used the neurons of reading a as its main test (38 of 39) with neurons N as a variant, so the outcome is unchanged, and reading b is now shown.
deviations: The areas of a session are those of its neurons as the Methods define a neuron, with the readings of edtable1-region-counts (criterion as amended); neurons N and all curated units are variants.

Assumption. A unit labelled with a finer Allen division (SCig, SCsg, LSr, LSc, ORBm, COA, TT, PIR, DP; 2,262 units) lies in its parent region among the 42 (Allen CCF hierarchy). The paper does not say how labels were grouped.

outcomes.statement: 60.0% of neurons (13,466) were significantly modulated during the task; of these 74.3% consistently increased and 20.2% consistently decreased their activity.
outcomes.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2
outcomes.quote: A sizeable fraction of all neurons (60.0%, 13,466 neurons) had significant modulation of firing rate during the task. Most of these neurons (74.3%) consistently increased their activity during the task, but a sizeable minority (20.2%) consistently decreased
outcomes.notes: On the criterion's neurons, every neuron (curated, at least 0.1 Hz) of the 42 regions (22,434), 13,532 have a test below 0.05/6 (60.32%). Under reading a 74.87% consistently increase and 20.95% decrease; under reading b 71.53% and 19.49%. All four values are within tolerance under both readings. The first run used neurons N (22,273), now a variant, with 13,439 active (60.34%), 74.95% and 20.89%. The active fraction by subject ranges from 50.4% to 73.2%. With labels as given, 12,263 of 20,418 neurons N_raw (60.06%) are active.
deviations: Rates are spike counts in each window divided by its length; the code (kernelFitBasic.m) interpolates binned rates. Tests that return no p-value because all values are equal (0 to 874 neurons per test) count as not significant, where the code keeps the neuron as included (its "BUG" comment).

Test 6 compares post-reward rates of correct NoGo trials (no stimulus, NoGo, positive feedback) with the baseline rates of all trials T, as kernelFitBasic.m does (ranksum of rewRates against bslRates).
Neurons are those of the criterion (all neurons of the 42 regions with a rate of at least 0.1 Hz); the first run used neurons N, now a variant.

outcomes.statement: Statistically responsive neurons have higher baseline firing rates than other neurons (d' = 0.35 ± 0.04), while their spike amplitudes differ much less (d' = 0.10 ± 0.02).
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 2 legend
outcomes.quote: Significant cells tend to have higher baseline firing rates ... while differences in spike amplitude are much smaller
outcomes.notes: Responsive neurons (any test below 0.05/6, neurons N) have higher baseline rates, d' = 0.392 ± 0.012 under reading a (0.002 above the bound of 0.35 ± 0.04) and 0.316 ± 0.013 under reading b (within tolerance). The amplitude d', with the mean waveform's peak-to-trough (the criterion's mean spike waveform amplitude), is 0.201 ± 0.014 (a) and 0.169 ± 0.038 (b), above 0.10 ± 0.02; with the file's spike_amps, the first run's measure and now a variant, 0.050 ± 0.013 and 0.060 ± 0.028, below. No reading has both values within tolerance, and the criterion gives no partial outcome; the first run recorded partially_reproduced. The direction holds under every measure and reading, the amplitude d' being smaller than the rate d'. The two amplitudes correlate at r = 0.685 over neurons.
deviations: Amplitude is the peak-to-trough of the unit's waveform_mean on the channel where it is largest; the mean of spike_amps (the template-based peak-to-trough of each spike) is a variant. The legend does not say which amplitude, and the file gives no unit for either.

outcomes.statement: When the mouse chose a contralateral stimulus, activity arose first in visual cortex and superficial superior colliculus and then spread to most regions; when it chose an ipsilateral stimulus, VIS and SCs were among the last areas to respond.
outcomes.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 2; Fig. 2d,e
outcomes.quote: When a mouse successfully selected a visual stimulus contralateral to the recorded hemisphere, activity emerged first in classical visual regions such as visual cortex (VIS) and superficial superior colliculus (SCs), and soon spread to most of the remaining recorded regions ... VIS and SCs were now amongst the last areas to respond
outcomes.notes: With the half-maximum latency (L1) and each responsive reading, VISp is the first region on correct contralateral trials (77.5 ms; rank percentile 0.024), SCs at percentile 0.061 to 0.083 (82.5 to 87.5 ms) and the VIS mean at 0.195 to 0.214; on ipsilateral trials VISp is at 0.73 to 0.95 and SCs at 0.70 to 0.78, in the latest third. With the time of the maximum (L2) SCs falls at 0.42 to 0.56 on contralateral trials, so the claim holds under L1 only. Regions need 5 responsive neurons (41 or 42 regions).
deviations: Contralateral correct trials are Right choices (T) on a right stimulus alone, matched in contrast with contralateral Miss and passive trials of the same single-stimulus type (definition M applied to these three groups). Sessions without matched trials contribute nothing.
The sliding-window display selection (reading a) uses windows starting 0 to 0.3 s after stimulus onset; the Methods do not give the range.

outcomes.statement: On Miss trials with a contralateral stimulus, activity appeared in a visual pathway of visual areas, basal ganglia and several midbrain structures but did not spread to the whole brain; on Miss trials with an ipsilateral stimulus there was essentially no activity.
outcomes.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 2; Fig. 2f,g
outcomes.quote: activity was found in a “visual pathway” consisting of classical visual areas, basal ganglia, and several midbrain structures ... but failed to propagate globally. When the mouse missed an ipsilateral stimulus, essentially no activity was seen in the recorded hemisphere
outcomes.notes: No reading meets all three conditions, and the criterion gives no partial outcome; the first run recorded partially_reproduced. With Z1 and finite z only, (i) holds (3.39% of visual-pathway neurons activated on contralateral Miss trials against 1.29% elsewhere) and (ii) holds (6.75% against 1.29% outside the pathway on Go and Miss), but (iii) fails: ipsilateral Miss 1.1868% (all sessions) against contralateral Miss 2.3658%, half being 1.1829%. With the two Miss sets matched to each other in contrast and count on the same 8,598 neurons of the 19 sessions (219 trials a side), ipsilateral 1.117% against contralateral 2.082% (half 1.041%), so (iii) fails by more; in the 14 sessions with at least 10 matched pairs, 1.281% against 2.378%. With Z2 and finite z, (ii) and (iii) hold and (i) fails (0.047% against 0.060%). The readings counting an infinite z (21.6% of neurons on Go trials have no baseline spikes) mark those neurons significant whatever they do and carry no information. Only 19 of 39 sessions have 10 matched single-stimulus trials per group.
deviations: The z of definition R is infinite for a neuron with no spikes in any baseline window. The paper does not say how such neurons are treated; both treatments (counted significant, or not) are run. The question is recorded for the authors (findings).
Matched trials are single-stimulus trials, as for fig2de; sessions with fewer than 10 matched trials per group are left out of the matched conditions.

Condition (iii) is also tested with contralateral and ipsilateral Miss trials matched to each other in contrast and count, on the same neurons of the same sessions; the criterion does not say whether the ipsilateral Miss trials are matched.

outcomes.statement: More neurons were significantly activated by contralateral visual stimuli on Miss trials in the task than on passive trials with the same contrasts, and passive responses were weaker than those on Miss trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 1; Fig. 5b; Fig. 2h
outcomes.quote: more neurons were significantly activated by visual stimuli during the task (Miss trials), than in the passive trials
outcomes.notes: More neurons are activated on matched Miss than passive trials under Z1 with finite z, pooled 4.82% against 3.24% (Figs. 3 to 5 set) and 3.30% against 2.52% (every neuron of the 42 regions at 0.1 Hz or more, the criterion's reading b; neurons N, now a variant, 3.30% against 2.51%), with Miss above passive in 30 and 29 of 42 regions. Under Z2 with finite z both fractions are near zero (0.05% and 0.04%) and the excess is positive in 3 or 4 regions. The infinite-z readings carry no information (21% of neurons counted without baseline spikes). The matched-contrast selection keeps 36 sessions with at least 10 trials per group (38 if counted over the three groups), not the 34 the criterion requires, and the criterion gives no partial outcome; the first run recorded partially_reproduced. The dropped sessions are Lederberg 2017-12-05, 2017-12-06 and 2017-12-07, with 0 to 4 NoGo trials at each contralateral contrast (0, 5 and 6 matched trials per group). Among the kept sessions the fewest matched trials are 10 (Lederberg 2017-12-10) and 14 (Lederberg 2017-12-11, Tatum 2017-12-06), so no threshold from 10 to 14 gives 34 either. All 39 sessions have at least 12 Left, Right and NoGo trials of definition T. Whether the session count should decide a claim about activation is asked of a reader (questions/steinmetz-2019.yaml); the claim is tested as the claims file has it.
deviations: The infinite z of neurons without baseline spikes is treated both ways, as in fig2fg.
The Methods say "When fewer than 10 such trials could be found, the session was excluded" without saying whether per group or in all; both are run, and neither gives 34.

outcomes.statement: Before the stimulus, neocortex and sensory thalamus were less active in the task than in the passive context, while basal ganglia and other subcortical choice areas were more active; VISp was lower and CP higher on Miss trials than on passive trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 1; Fig. 5a,c; Extended Data Fig. 9a; Methods, Engagement Index and pre-stimulus analyses
outcomes.quote: While neocortex and sensory thalamus showed a net decrease in pre-stimulus activity during task context, other regions ... showed a consistent increase
outcomes.notes: Under factor reading a (the Methods' nested ANOVA) with all passive events, 23 regions differ at p < 0.0012; all 9 differing neocortical regions (ACA, MOp, ORB, SSp, VISa, VISam, VISl, VISp, VISrl) are lower in the task, the visual thalamus (LD, LGd, LP) is lower too, and all 11 other differing regions (ACB, CA1, CA3, CP, DG, GPe, LS, MRN, SNr, VPM, ZI) are higher. VISp is lower on matched Miss than passive trials (1.64 against 2.39 Hz) and CP higher (3.10 against 2.77 Hz) in window a, likewise in window b. Factor reading b gives 14 differing regions with the same pattern. With passive visual presentations and factors a, ILA is higher in the task, so that reading fails.
deviations: Under factor reading a, the condition F of a model with condition and neuron nested in session, with one observation per neuron and condition, equals the square of the paired t across neurons, which is how it is computed.
The VISp and CP comparison uses the sessions kept for definition M (36).

outcomes.statement: Pre-stimulus firing in midbrain, basal ganglia and hippocampal regions is ordered Passive < Miss < Go, while in neocortical areas it is higher in Passive than in Miss and Go.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 6b legend
outcomes.quote: the pre-stimulus firing rate of midbrain, basal ganglia, and hippocampal regions is in the order Passive < Miss < Go; whereas pre-stimulus activity in neocortical areas instead is arranged as Passive > Miss and Go
outcomes.notes: In window a 11 of 15 midbrain, basal ganglia and hippocampal regions show Passive < Miss < Go and 12 of 14 neocortical regions have Passive above Miss and Go; window b gives 12 of 15 and 12 of 14.

outcomes.statement: Regions whose pre-stimulus rate differed between task and passive contexts showed similar differences between Go and Miss trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 2; Fig. 5d
outcomes.quote: Areas that showed differences in pre-stimulus firing rate between task and passive contexts also showed similar differences between Go and Miss trials
outcomes.notes: Across 42 regions the task minus passive difference and the Go minus Miss difference correlate with r = 0.641 (window a) and 0.622 (window b), p below 1e-4; Spearman 0.639 and 0.636. With all neurons N of each region, the reading of the Fig. 5d legend ("averaged over all neurons in a region", 130 to 1534 neurons), r = 0.494 (p = 0.0009) and 0.507 (p = 0.0006), also reproduced. Whether the criterion should use all neurons is asked in questions/steinmetz-2019.yaml.

outcomes.statement: The pre-stimulus detect probability of each area correlated with its task minus passive difference (r = 0.48, p = 0.001), as the Go minus Miss difference does.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 7f legend
outcomes.quote: The pre-stimulus Detect Probability was correlated with the Engagement Index (i.e. Task-Passive difference) similarly to the Go-Miss difference (with r = 0.48, p=0.001; not shown)
outcomes.notes: The correlation across 42 areas between the mean pre-stimulus detect probability minus 0.5 and the task minus passive difference is r = 0.515 (p = 0.0005, window a) and 0.488 (p = 0.0011, window b), both within 0.48 ± 0.048. With all neurons N of each region (the fig5d question), r = 0.444 (p = 0.0032) and 0.442 (p = 0.0034), also within tolerance (lower bound 0.432). The question is asked in questions/steinmetz-2019.yaml.

outcomes.statement: An engagement index, the projection of pre-stimulus population activity onto the task minus passive difference vector, was higher on Go than on Miss trials consistently across recordings (mean difference 8.42 a.u., paired t-test p < 1e-4).
outcomes.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 2; Fig. 5f; Methods, Engagement Index and pre-stimulus analyses
outcomes.quote: This engagement index differed between Go and Miss trials consistently across recordings ... paired t-test
outcomes.notes: With trials T and contralateral contrast above zero (readings a, a), Go exceeds Miss by 7.85 a.u. on average (s.e. 1.54; positive in 29 of 36 sessions), paired t = 5.09, p = 1.2e-5, with 344 ± 34 neurons per session (mean ± s.e.); expected 8.42 ± 0.84 and 319 ± 32.5. All task trials for the vector (b, a) give 8.06. Including zero contrast (contrast reading b) gives 4.69 (p = 2.2e-4), outside tolerance. The regions are those of the Methods' ANOVA reading in fig5c; the region sets of the other readings give 6.69 to 7.92 with p below 1e-4. The test and the mean hold as the criterion requires; the session count is 36, not the expected 34, because the matched-contrast selection keeps 36 (fig5b).
deviations: Sessions are those kept for definition M (36), the paper's 34 sessions could not be identified.
Go and Miss trials are those of definition T; the index uses the window -0.2 to 0 s on every task trial without dropping trials with movement, as the Methods' paragraph does not drop them.

outcomes.statement: The probability of a Go response rises with the engagement index on single trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 2; Fig. 5e
outcomes.quote: it was possible to predict whether an animal would respond to the stimulus on a given trial within the task context, by projecting pre-stimulus population activity onto a weight vector given by the difference of pre-stimulus activity in passive and task contexts
outcomes.notes: On 2,434 matched trials the logistic slope of Go on the index is 0.44 (95% interval 0.35 to 0.53) with z-scoring within session and 0.19 (0.11 to 0.27) over all trials. P(Go) rises from 0.335 to 0.614 across quintiles.

outcomes.statement: The engagement index improves the prediction of Go responses beyond inter-trial interval, previous reward, pupil area and motion energy (deviance test, p = 1.5e-8).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 9i legend; Methods, GLM prediction of P(Go) from pre-stimulus variables
outcomes.quote: The null hypothesis that engagement index had no additional effect on Go probability over all other variables was rejected using a deviance test (p=1.5e-8)
outcomes.notes: Adding the index lowers the deviance by 63.1 (1 d.f., p = 2.0e-15) in window a and 64.0 (p = 1.2e-15) in window b, one GLM over 34 sessions and 2,350 trials; one GLM per session gives a summed drop of 169.7 over 34 d.f. (p = 6.0e-20). The paper reports p = 1.5e-8. The p-value is smaller here than in the paper.
deviations: Inter-trial interval is stimulus onset minus the previous trial's feedback time, a standard choice; the Methods do not define it.

Sessions are those kept for definition M with pupil data (34; 2.9% of matched trials lack a pupil value and are dropped). The paper excluded 5 sessions for unusable pupil video, which the dandiset does not identify.

outcomes.statement: The Go against Miss difference in engagement index persists on trials after rewards, after regressing out previous reward, and on trials after short and after long inter-trial intervals.

outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds the CCF coordinates and region of every channel, but no DiI spot coordinates, histology images or electrophysiological landmarks, which the measures need. The files and the dandiset metadata were searched; the figshare deposit the paper names (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.9598406) was not examined, and the claims file does not name it as the source of these data.

findings.statement: The `rate` attribute of the `starting_time` of `wheel_position`, `lickPiezo` and `face_motion_energy` holds the sampling interval in seconds (0.0004, 0.002 and 0.0253), not a rate in Hz. Sample counts times these values give the recording lengths (2,609 to 4,103 s), so a reader that takes the attribute as a rate in Hz gets every sample time wrong.

`units/peak_channel` is 1-based: the electrodes row peak_channel - 1 matches the unit's cluster depth (median difference 8.0 um, against 13.4 um for row peak_channel). The description does not say so, and a unit's region depends on it.

`wheel_moves` is an IntervalSeries whose `data` (the movement type) has half the length of its `timestamps`, which hold each movement's onset and offset in turn; an IntervalSeries should have one data value per timestamp.

Channel locations mix levels of the Allen hierarchy. 2,262 curated units carry finer labels (SCig, LSr, COA, TT, SCsg, ORBm, LSc, PIR, DP) whose parents are among the paper's 42 regions, and others carry broad labels (TH, MB, CA). The paper's counts per region are recovered only after mapping the finer labels to their parents, which the dandiset does not document.
Genotypes are written differently from Supplementary Table 1 (Ai95 x VGlut1-Cre for RCL-GCaMP6f x VGlut-Cre, Vglut1-Cre for Vglut1-IRES2-Cre-D); sexes, ages and the 39 sessions match the paper.
The Methods exclude 5 of 39 sessions from the pupil analyses for unusable video, but the dandiset does not say which; eye_area is present in all 39 files, with missing values in two.

`spike_amps` and `waveform_mean` give no unit, and the trial table's `included` flag (engaged trials) differs from the Methods' disengagement rule on 1.7% of trials, although it gives the paper's 9,538 trials exactly.
The dandiset holds no histology (DiI spot coordinates, slice images) or electrophysiological landmarks, so the probe localization of the Methods cannot be checked.

The kernel model of the paper's code runs on the dandiset: with the basis of CanonCor2all.m and the elastic net of the Methods, 2,886 of 13,852 task-responsive neurons pass the 2% cross-validated VE of the nested tests, against about 4,240 in the paper, so counts of kernel-requiring neurons come out lower than the paper's. Following four details of the code's fits (one glmnet fit on all basis columns, truncated; no intercept; VE from the variance of the residuals; glmnet's scaling of the ridge term) raises the count to 3,199; the rest of the gap is unexplained.

disagreements.reason: Keep the verified outcome. The numbers come from the data and there is no sign of cherry-picking, but the criterion is written for one shuffle, as in the paper (Methods, "Estimation of false positive rate"), and the tolerance was already sized for the spread of a single shuffle, so using the mean of five shuffles changes the criterion. The change was made after seeing the result: the averaging came only after the first shuffle had failed, and the fallback (0.19%) uses a variant reading, while the main fits give 0.14%. At this attempt's lower rate the 1-to-12 range of single counts is about what Poisson noise predicts. Even taking five shuffles, the result is not clearly a reproduction: 2 of 5 single shuffles within tolerance under the main fits, pooled 31 of 14,317 neurons, 0.217%, Poisson 95% interval about 0.15% to 0.31%, which spans the 0.16% lower bound and does not include 0.33%. Caution still open: only 2,886 neurons enter the nested tests under the main fits (3,199 under the code's reading) against about 4,240; the lower rate may come from this attempt's model.

paper_notes.statement: Question for the authors. Definition R (Methods, Data analysis) z-scores the mean rate 0 to 0.25 s against the trial baselines -0.1 to 0 s. For about 21% of neurons on matched single-stimulus trials no baseline window has a spike, so the z is infinite. Were such neurons counted as significant, left out, or was a variance floor used? Counting them, 17% to 23% of neurons are significant on contralateral Miss trials; leaving them out, 2% to 5% (Z1; fig2fg, fig5b).

Question for the authors. The matched-contrast selection (Methods, Training protocol) excludes sessions "When fewer than 10 such trials could be found", leaving 34 of 39. Here 36 sessions have at least 10 matched trials per group (Lederberg 2017-12-05, 2017-12-06 and 2017-12-07 are dropped) and 38 have 10 over the three groups; the next fewest are 10 and 14 trials. Which count was meant, and which further two sessions were removed?

Question for the authors. "94.1% ± 0.6% of trials with high contrast stimuli had no movement" in the passive replay: which window and which movements count? With the dataset's detected movements of any kind, 84.6% of high-contrast passive presentations have none in -0.05 to 0.4 s.

Question for the authors. Fig. 3d and 3e give the fraction of neurons in each region requiring a kernel and leave empty the regions where "the number of neurons passing analysis criteria was < 5". Is the denominator the neurons that entered the nested tests (full-model VE of at least 2%), or every neuron of the region in the analysis? Here the first reading reproduces fig3d-vision-localized (the five highest fractions all in visual areas) and the second does not (CP enters the five highest); no region has fewer than 5 neurons under the second.

entries.title: Choice, action and engagement across the mouse brain (Steinmetz et al. 2019)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Steinmetz, Zatka-Haas, Carandini and Harris (2019) on dandiset 000017, which holds Neuropixels recordings from 39 sessions of 10 mice performing a visual discrimination task, with passive replay. It covers the behaviour, the counts of neurons and regions, task responsiveness, the spread of activity after the stimulus, the pre-stimulus engagement signal, detect probability, the jPECC lead-lag analysis and the kernel regression. The decoding from kernel-model residuals was not run.
